title: Concurrency & distribution — where it stands
eyebrow: Capability positioning · read from the source, not from memory
thesis: An unusual shape: the substrates are complete and excellent, while the vocabulary over them is design-only. Three sub-planes ship, each heavily guarded with real multi-process tests — message-passing nodes with OTP-style supervision (the pragmatic 80% of Erlang: mailboxes, location-transparent Send/Ask, restart budgets, heartbeats, topology-as-data); a measured-gated multicore tier (bit-identical or justified, elementwise killed by the memory wall); and an elastic HTTP worker fleet with a smart router and autoscaling — over a full libuv reactor with mTLS. What's not built is the plane's own headline: the one "routing vocabulary" (`Concurrently()`) that would let you say "do this concurrently" and have it land on the right substrate.
grid_title: Twelve lanes, each against its category leader
grid_lede: Every lane names what actually ships, the tools it is fair to measure against, and the one thing still owed. The six Strong lanes are the shipped, guarded substrates; the honest gap is the ergonomic layer that would unify them.

lanes.engine: Share-nothing nodes (`stzNode`) with an engine-enforced bounded inbox (counted overflow: drop-oldest / drop-newest / refuse), `On(tag,f)` dispatch, and a registry (`stzNodePlane`) giving location-transparent `Send` (fire-forget) and `Ask` (reply, mandatory timeout) over an in-house STZM wire codec.
lanes.owed: Guarded with real OS processes (D0–D2): FIFO-by-content, exact overflow counts, byte-identical results local vs remote. Genuinely Erlang-shaped for a non-BEAM language.

lanes.engine: `stzNodeSupervisor`: `:OneForOne` / `:AllForOne` strategies, a restart budget (max/window) with escalation, heartbeats that catch a wedged node, and death-notice monitors — pure policy over engine observations, hostable on an agent host.
lanes.owed: Proven by surviving vs wiped state under real kills (D3): OneForOne preserves a sibling, AllForOne resets it, budget escalates, heartbeats catch the wedge. OTP-grade supervision, guarded.

lanes.engine: Share-nothing OS processes exchanging STZM frames over reactor TCP/mTLS, addressed by name, supervised. Topology as data (`Describe()` emits plain nested lists; handlers are Ring code strings so they cross a process boundary); `Deploy` moves a node in one line.
lanes.owed: Complete and guarded end-to-end (D4–D6, a semantic-search node Deploy'd and killed mid-run). It is process-pool + message-passing distribution — the pragmatic 80% of Erlang — not Ray-class dynamic task graphs (lane 11).

lanes.engine: Five parallel sites, each a `std.Thread.spawn` behind a measured `calib.Gate` (failed spawn computes inline): row-banded matmul, gated-parallel LU, compensated threaded reductions, and kNN / distance scans — 2.7–6.7×, transparent (the user never asks).
lanes.owed: Correctness is two-class: partition-output is bit-identical (asserted), reduce-across-threads carries a written justification. Elementwise was killed — the memory wall (one core already pulls ~39 of ~58 GB/s).

lanes.engine: `reactor.zig` — vendored libuv on its own thread, a submit→ticket→await idiom where no callback crosses into Ring: async timers, TCP, subprocess (with kill), curl HTTPS, and HTTP/STZM/TLS listeners, plus a reactor pool of N loops.
lanes.owed: A genuine async runtime with a clean no-VM-callback model and mTLS termination. The ergonomic surface over it (channels, structured concurrency) is the vocabulary gap (lane 12).

lanes.engine: An elastic HTTP fleet: `stzWorkerPool` (admission / load-isolation), a 3-tier `stzRequestClassifier` (rules / lexical / model), `stzAppCluster` (front host + worker processes via reactor spawn+curl), `stzClusterSupervisor` (autoscale on live `/health`), staged `stzComputePipeline`, and p50–p99 telemetry.
lanes.owed: Guarded with a real 3-process fleet (health-wait, round-robin, teardown). A Ray-Serve-shaped fleet for HTTP facets — the reach is live multi-machine verification (Tier C).

lanes.engine: Retry-with-failover + per-worker circuit breakers, token-bucket rate limiting, at-most-once delivery (late replies discarded by correlation id), mandatory timeouts, `Drain`/`Stop` — with a hardening guard against SSRF, CRLF smuggling and injection.
lanes.owed: A real resilience toolkit, guarded — but fleet-scoped; the general per-call policy vocabulary (bulkheads, adaptive concurrency) is thinner than a dedicated service mesh.

lanes.engine: HTTP client (sync `http.zig` + async reactor curl), TCP client/server (blocking `tcp.zig` + async reactor TCP), URL parsing and DNS — HTTP framing fuzzed and property-tested.
lanes.owed: No UDP, WebSocket is still curl-based (not a native implementation), and the plain client/server faces are blocking. HTTP/TCP are covered; the edges are not.

lanes.engine: Mutual TLS via vendored mbedTLS in the reactor: server termination with `require_client`, a client role (`reactor_connect_tls`, link-up only on completed handshake), and a reactor-free smoke guard (`mtls_smoke.zig`, exit-code gated).
lanes.owed: Real mutual auth, but test certs only — no cert lifecycle, rotation, OCSP or real-CA verification story. It proves the handshake, not a managed PKI.

lanes.engine: `stzComputeFederation`: a governed multi-host constellation — `Join(host,endpoint,facets)`, a governance lattice (risk/grant/authority), and `FederatedCall` (discovered → governed → transported over reactor async curl).
lanes.owed: Unified at the vocabulary level (one signer, one lattice, one TLS channel) but facet discovery is still HTTP, not re-expressed over the node plane (D5 residue) — and it is governed remote-call, not a distributed scheduler.

lanes.engine: Distribution today routes named work — messages to nodes, requests to facet workers. Arbitrary task submission with data-dependency scheduling is not built.
lanes.owed: No Ray-style dynamic task graph — submit an arbitrary function, let a scheduler place it and track its dependencies. The plan explicitly refuses this until a workload earns it; message-passing is the deliberate model.

lanes.engine: A detailed plan of record (CN0–CN5): one adverb `Concurrently()`, a `stzTask` / ticket / `stzWorkshop` surface that routes work to the right substrate (engine threads / reactor / processes) by declaration + measurement, never guessed. No code exists — `base/concurrent/` holds only the plan; its test dir is empty.
lanes.owed: The plane's headline is unbuilt: the three substrates it would route over all ship, but the adverb, task, ticket and workshop that make concurrency ergonomic — and a channel/select primitive — do not.

gaps_title: The gaps, ordered by return — not by size
gaps_lede: Three tiers. The first builds the ergonomic layer the excellent substrates deserve; the second finishes the transport and networking edges; the third is the scheduler and PKI reach.

tiers.title: Tier A — the ergonomic layer the substrates deserve

items.title: Build the routing vocabulary (CN0–CN5)
items.text: `Concurrently()` + `stzTask` / ticket / `stzWorkshop` that route to engine threads, the reactor, or processes by declaration and measured break-even. Three strong substrates exist; this is the single move that makes them one usable concurrency model.

items.title: Channels & structured concurrency
items.text: A first-class channel / select primitive and scoped task groups over the mailbox + reactor substrates — the Go/structured-concurrency ergonomics that make fan-out and coordination readable rather than hand-wired.

items.title: Federation over the node plane
items.text: Re-express `stzComputeFederation` discovery/transport over the node registry (the D5 residue), so distribution is one message plane rather than HTTP-discovery plus node-plane split.

items.title: UDP & a native WebSocket
items.text: A UDP surface and a first-party WebSocket (today it rides curl `CONNECT_ONLY`) — the two networking edges the HTTP/TCP core leaves open.

items.title: A managed-PKI mTLS story
items.text: Beyond test certs and a handshake: cert lifecycle, rotation, real-CA verification and OCSP — so mutual TLS is deployable, not just demonstrable.

items.title: Dynamic task-graph distribution
items.text: Ray-style arbitrary-task submission with dependency scheduling across the fleet — deliberately refused today. Strategic if a workload needs a distributed scheduler rather than named message-passing.

items.title: Live multi-machine verification
items.text: The fleet and federation are proven on local processes; running and verifying them across real machines (and the deploy plane's ssh/registry backends with them) makes "distributed" true in fact, not just in loopback.

items.title: The refused-until-measured multicore sites
items.text: Parallel Cholesky / QR / back-substitution — held back because their reductions sit under the oracle tolerances. Admit them once a measurement makes the correctness case, as the tier's own discipline requires.

notes.lead: The honesty line on the ratings.
notes.text: Re-surveyed from `main`. The substrates are guarded with real multi-process tests — D0–D6 spawn 2–6 OS processes, D3 performs real kills, R8 runs a 3-process fleet — proving FIFO-by-content, exact overflow counts, location-transparency by byte-identical results, restart-by-surviving-state and at-most-once. Two test-runner artifacts to note: the cluster `_ERR_RUN.txt` shows one error for a file that does not exist in the tree (a stale harness entry; the 20+ narrated guards aren't in that record), and the network `_ERR_RUN.txt` ran only 2 of ~26 suites. And `base/concurrent/` is genuinely empty — the routing vocabulary does not exist yet.

Softanza has category-competitive concurrency substrates — Erlang-shaped supervised nodes, a measured multicore tier, an elastic worker fleet, a real async reactor — and lacks the ergonomic vocabulary that would let a user reach them without knowing which one they're using; the plane's own headline is its one big gap.
